questions.stem: Which of these is a language feature rather than a text structure?
options: A shift from first-person narration to third-person in part two
High-modality verbs such as 'must' and 'will' throughout a speech
A cyclical ending that returns to the opening image
Subheadings that divide a feature article into stages
questions.explanation: Language features are choices at the level of words and sentences — modality, imagery, sentence length, tone. The other three all describe how the whole text is organised or sequenced, which is structure. The cyclical ending is the most tempting because it involves an image, but the analytical point is about where the image is placed in the text's shape, not about the wording itself.

questions.stem: Two students analyse the same line, "The developers came, and the wetland went." Which statement analyses both a language feature and its effect?
options: The line is about developers destroying a wetland, which shows the writer supports environmental protection
The word 'went' is a past-tense verb, and past tense is used because the events have already happened
The parallel clause structure equates arrival and loss, making the destruction sound routine and inevitable
The line uses a compound sentence joined by 'and', which is a common feature of persuasive writing
questions.explanation: A complete analysis names a specific choice — here the mirrored clause pattern — and states what it does to the reader's understanding. Identifying the compound sentence is accurate labelling but stops before any effect, so it is description rather than analysis. The test: after naming the feature, can you finish the sentence 'which makes the reader...'?

questions.stem: In a small-group discussion, Ravi and Elif disagree about whether a memoir's short, fragmented sentences signal trauma or simply a plain style. What is the most productive next move for the group?
options: Return to a sampled passage and test each reading against where the fragments cluster in the text
Take a vote so the group can record one agreed interpretation and move on to the next question
Accept both readings as equally valid, since interpretation of style is a matter of personal taste
Ask the teacher which reading is correct, because disagreement means the group has misread the text
questions.explanation: Analytical disagreement is resolved by returning to evidence: if fragments cluster around the traumatic episodes rather than appearing evenly, one reading is better supported than the other. Accepting both as equally valid is tempting because interpretations can differ, but readings are not equal when the text supports one more strongly — 'taste' is not the standard in textual analysis. The cue is that a productive discussion move sends the group back to the text, not away from it.

questions.stem: An opinion piece opens with a one-sentence anecdote about a child waiting at a bus stop, then moves into statistics, then closes by returning to the child. What is the purpose of this text structure?
options: It shows the piece is a narrative rather than a persuasive text, since it tells a story
It makes the article chronological, so events are presented in the order they happened
It frames the argument with a human example so the statistics are read as affecting real people
It signals that the writer is uncertain about the statistics and is hedging the claim
questions.explanation: A circular or 'bookend' structure returns to an opening image so the reader interprets the evidence in the middle through that human frame, strengthening the persuasive appeal. The tempting option is the claim that a story makes the text a narrative, but persuasive writing frequently uses anecdote as a technique without changing genre. Ask what the structure does for the argument, not just what kind of material it contains.

questions.stem: Two students analyse the same review. Josh says the short paragraphs make the review easy to skim; Nadia says they make the writer seem dismissive of the film. What is the best way for the group to resolve this in discussion?
options: Take a vote, because a class discussion should settle on one interpretation before moving on
Accept Josh's view, because effects on readability are objective while tone is only opinion
Discard both readings, because paragraph length is a structural choice with no effect at all
Test both readings against specific paragraphs, since a feature can create more than one effect
questions.explanation: Text structures can produce several effects at once, so the productive move is to return to the text and check which readings the evidence supports. The tempting option is preferring Josh's view as 'objective', but claims about readability are interpretive too and require evidence just as claims about tone do. In discussion, evidence resolves disagreement; voting and ranking types of claim do not.

questions.stem: A speaker in a panel discussion says: "I hear you saying the ending is bleak, but could the bleakness itself be the point? What in the final paragraph made you read it as hopeless?" Which interaction skill is most clearly demonstrated?
options: Conceding the point in order to keep the discussion polite and avoid open disagreement
Restating the other speaker's view accurately without adding any new interpretation
Redirecting the group away from the ending towards a different section of the text
Challenging an interpretation while inviting the other speaker to supply textual evidence
questions.explanation: The speaker offers an alternative reading and then asks a question that sends the other speaker back to the text, which is how discussion moves from opinion to analysis. The tempting option is 'restating without adding', because the turn does begin by paraphrasing, but the paraphrase is only a lead-in to a counter-reading and a request for evidence. Look at what the turn does overall, not just how it opens.

questions.stem: In a spoken text, which set of choices are all "features of voice"?
options: Slides, captions, background music and images
Topic sentences, connectives and a summarising conclusion
Pace, pitch, volume and pausing
Gesture, eye contact, posture and facial expression
questions.explanation: Features of voice are the vocal or paralinguistic choices a speaker controls while speaking — how fast, how high or low, how loud, and where silence falls. Gesture, eye contact, posture and facial expression are tempting, but these are body language or non-verbal features, not voice; you could hear a speech on radio and lose them entirely while the voice features remain. The cue is the ear test: if it survives with your eyes shut, it is a feature of voice.

questions.stem: A student gives a formal address at assembly, to staff, students and parents. Which register suits?
options: Contractions and casual asides throughout, to keep the tone conversational
Standard Australian English with full forms and few colloquialisms
Heavy slang and in-jokes, so the student audience feels it is authentic
Technical jargon throughout, so the speech sounds authoritative to everyone
questions.explanation: Formality is matched to context: an assembly with mixed adult and student listeners calls for standard English, careful phrasing and restrained colloquial language so all listeners are included and the occasion is respected. Constant contractions and casual asides is the tempting option because informality can build rapport, but sustained casualness across a formal ceremonial occasion misreads the audience and lowers credibility. Ask who is listening and what the occasion expects before setting register.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of deliberately pausing after a key statistic in a persuasive speech?
options: To reduce the total speaking time so the speech fits the time limit
To correct a mistake in pronunciation made in the previous sentence
To give the audience a moment to absorb the point and to mark its importance
To signal to the audience that the speaker has finished the whole speech
questions.explanation: A pause functions as spoken punctuation: it separates ideas and gives emphasis, letting listeners process a striking figure before the next point arrives. Signalling the end of the speech is tempting because a long final silence does close a speech, but a mid-speech pause after evidence marks emphasis, not conclusion. Judge a pause by where it falls — after key content it emphasises, after the final line it closes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a multimodal or digital element in a spoken presentation?
options: A rhetorical question addressed directly to the audience
A rise in volume on the final word of a sentence
A three-part structure of problem, evidence and solution
An embedded short video clip played behind the speaker
questions.explanation: Multimodal elements add a mode beyond the spoken word — visual, audio or digital material such as video, slides, infographics or sound. A rhetorical question is tempting because it feels like an interactive technique, but it is delivered purely through spoken language and so belongs to rhetoric, not to mode. Check whether the audience receives information through an additional channel; if not, it is not multimodal.

questions.stem: Ana is presenting research findings to a panel of teachers and then adapting the same content into a two-minute talk for Year 7 students. Which adaptation best shows deliberate consideration of the second audience?
options: Replacing technical terms with everyday comparisons and shortening her sentences
Keeping the wording identical but speaking more loudly so younger students hear
Cutting all visual support so the younger students concentrate on her words
Adding more statistics so the younger audience sees the research is credible
questions.explanation: Adapting for audience means changing language and structure so meaning is accessible: plain wording, concrete comparisons and shorter sentences match younger listeners' processing. Speaking more loudly is tempting because volume is a genuine delivery choice, but volume does not make unfamiliar technical vocabulary comprehensible — it only makes it louder. Ask whether the change alters what the audience can understand, not merely what they can hear.

questions.stem: A student's slides for an eight-minute speech contain full paragraphs of text that he reads aloud word for word. Why does this weaken the multimodal design of the presentation?
options: The slides mean the speech no longer counts as a structured spoken text
The slides prevent the speaker from using any features of voice at all
The slides duplicate the spoken mode instead of adding visual information to it
The slides make the presentation informal, which is unsuitable for a classroom
questions.explanation: Effective multimodal design uses each mode to do different work — the voice carries explanation while visuals carry images, data or key terms; duplicating the same words in both modes splits attention and adds nothing. Saying it is no longer a structured spoken text is tempting, but a read-aloud speech still has an introduction, body and conclusion, so structure is not what fails here. Test each slide by asking what it shows that the voice cannot say.

questions.stem: A student opens a speech to a local council meeting with: "Look, honestly, this whole thing's a bit of a joke." What is the most likely effect of this register choice on that audience?
options: It guarantees the councillors will find the speaker relatable and honest
It makes the speech informal, which is always inappropriate in any public setting
It shows the speaker has misunderstood the topic being debated at the meeting
It risks appearing disrespectful and reduces the speaker's credibility with councillors
questions.explanation: Register carries social meaning: dismissive colloquialism at a formal civic occasion signals a mismatch with the setting and can cost the speaker authority before the argument begins. Claiming informality is always inappropriate in public settings is tempting, but informality suits many public contexts such as a school fundraiser or a podcast — the problem is the mismatch with this audience, not informality itself. Judge register against the specific occasion, never as a universal rule.

questions.stem: A tourism campaign shows a stretch of coastline as empty golden sand at sunrise, with no people, buildings or roads in frame. How is place represented?
options: As dangerous and remote, which warns visitors to prepare carefully before travelling
As economically productive, because the image emphasises the industries of the coastline
As historically significant, because the sunrise signals a long record of settlement there
As untouched and available, which erases the people who live and work along that coast
questions.explanation: Framing decisions include what is left out; excluding residents, housing and infrastructure constructs the coast as pristine and open to the viewer, a common tourism convention. The "dangerous and remote" option confuses emptiness with hostility, but the warm light and calm sand code the scene as inviting rather than threatening. Always ask what an image omits, since absence is itself a representational choice.

questions.stem: Which question would best help a student evaluate, rather than simply describe, how a text represents homelessness?
options: Which specific words and images does the text use when it mentions homelessness?
How many paragraphs of the text deal with the topic of homelessness?
What does the writer say happens to the people described in the text?
Whose perspective on homelessness is centred, and whose is left out or spoken for?
questions.explanation: Evaluation involves judging a representation — asking about whose voice is included, whose is silenced and what effect that has — rather than cataloguing features. Asking which words and images are used is the strongest distractor, but that identifies evidence and stays at description until it is turned towards a judgement. Descriptive questions ask "what"; evaluative questions ask "whose", "why" and "at what cost".

questions.stem: Two documentaries about the same drought-affected town differ: one uses slow shots of cracked earth with sombre strings, the other uses time-lapse of a busy main street with upbeat guitar. What is the best conclusion?
options: Each constructs a different representation of the town by selecting and combining images and sound
One documentary must contain factual errors, since two versions of one town cannot both stand
The second documentary is more reliable because upbeat footage shows the town's real resilience
The difference is caused by filming conditions rather than by any deliberate choices
questions.explanation: Multimodal texts represent through selection: what is framed, how long a shot lasts and what music accompanies it all shape how an audience feels about the subject. The claim that one must contain errors is tempting because the two versions clash, but both can be factually true while representing the town in opposing ways. When two texts on one subject differ, look first at selection and emphasis rather than assuming one is lying.

questions.stem: A journalist describes a group of demonstrators as a 'horde'. Which term best names the language feature that carries the writer's attitude here?
options: Modality — the degree of certainty or obligation a word expresses
Nominalisation — turning a process or action into a noun
Connotation — the associations a word carries beyond its literal meaning
Denotation — the plain dictionary definition the word refers to
questions.explanation: 'Horde' literally refers to a large group, but it carries associations of disorder and threat, and it is those associations — the connotations — that position readers to view the demonstrators negatively. Denotation is tempting because the word does denote a crowd, but denotation is the neutral literal meaning and cannot by itself carry attitude. When a question asks where the attitude comes from, look past what the word points to and ask what it makes readers feel.

questions.stem: An editorial states: 'This reform must be passed immediately; there is no alternative.' What does the high modality in this sentence do?
options: It signals that the writer is open to other points of view
It provides evidence that no other policy option exists
It makes the writing more formal without affecting meaning
It presents the writer's belief as certain and beyond dispute
questions.explanation: High modality words such as 'must' and absolute phrasing such as 'no alternative' express strong commitment, so an opinion is presented as though it were an established fact. The option about formality is tempting because modality does affect tone, but the change here is to the strength of the claim, not merely its level of formality. Ask what the modal word does to the certainty of the claim, not just how it sounds.

questions.stem: A commentator writes: 'The company's so-called consultation lasted twenty minutes.' What attitude does the phrasing 'so-called' implicitly represent?
options: Uncertainty about exactly how long the meeting actually ran
Neutrality, since the writer reports only the length of the meeting
Scepticism that the process deserves to be described as consultation
Approval that the company met its consultation obligations quickly
questions.explanation: 'So-called' distances the writer from the label that follows, signalling that the term is being used by others but is not accepted as accurate, which positions readers to distrust the process. Claiming the sentence is neutral is tempting because it does contain a factual detail, but the fact sits inside an evaluative frame that undercuts the company. Watch for distancing devices such as 'so-called', 'supposed' and scare quotes — they carry judgement without stating it.

questions.stem: A media release reads: 'Errors were made during the approval process and delays were experienced.' How does this grammatical choice shape the representation of responsibility?
options: The plural nouns show that many separate people caused the problems
The passive constructions remove the agent, so no one is named as responsible
The passive constructions emphasise the agent by placing it at the end
The past tense shows the organisation has formally accepted the blame
questions.explanation: Passive voice allows the doer to be deleted entirely, so events appear to happen by themselves and accountability is quietly obscured. The option about emphasising the agent is tempting because passive voice can place an agent late in the sentence using 'by', but here there is no 'by' phrase at all, so nobody is named. Test any passive sentence by asking 'by whom?' — if the text never answers, responsibility has been hidden.

questions.stem: A news feature about a proposed mine quotes the company's chief executive and two government ministers at length, and includes no comment from local residents. What is the most defensible conclusion about the text's implicit values?
options: The absence of resident comment shows that local residents have no strong views about the proposal
The report is balanced, because it contains no emotive vocabulary and reports statements accurately
Voice selection is a structural matter only and cannot indicate the attitudes a text represents
The selection of voices privileges economic and official authority and marginalises those most affected
questions.explanation: Which voices are given space, and which are absent, is itself a language and composition choice that positions readers to accept some perspectives as authoritative. The 'balanced because there is no emotive vocabulary' option is tempting, since neutral wording often signals objectivity, but bias can operate entirely through selection and omission while every individual sentence stays calm. When judging representation, always ask who speaks, who is spoken about, and who is missing.

questions.stem: A text represents a value implicitly rather than explicitly when it:
options: conveys the attitude through connotation, word choice or emphasis without ever stating it directly
states the attitude in a clear topic sentence that the reader can quote as evidence
presents an attitude that most readers in the intended audience already happen to share
offers an attitude that the writer holds personally rather than one held by an institution
questions.explanation: Implicit representation means the values are carried by the language choices themselves — loaded words, what is emphasised, what is left out — so the reader infers them rather than reading them stated. The option about a clear topic sentence describes the opposite: explicit representation, where the position is spelled out on the page. The cue is where the meaning sits: on the surface of the sentence (explicit) or underneath the word choices (implicit). Whether an attitude is widely shared, or personal versus institutional, has nothing to do with the implicit/explicit distinction.

questions.stem: A council report describes bulldozing remnant bushland as 'site preparation' and describes residents' written objections as 'community feedback'. What do these word choices most clearly do?
options: Use emotive language to dramatise the clearing, implicitly representing the bushland as irreplaceable
Use euphemism to soften the actions, implicitly representing the project as routine and uncontroversial
Use technical jargon to exclude residents, explicitly representing the council as hostile to the public
Use high modality to insist on the project, implicitly representing opposition as legally unfounded
questions.explanation: 'Site preparation' and 'community feedback' are milder substitutes for destruction and objection, and euphemism of this kind makes a contested action sound like ordinary process — an attitude the reader infers rather than reads. The jargon option is tempting because these are institutional phrases, but they are not specialist terms and nothing in them explicitly declares hostility. Check modality words (must, will, certainly) before claiming high modality, and check for intensity before claiming emotive language: these phrases work by draining intensity, not adding it.

questions.stem: An energy company advertisement says: 'We all want cleaner air for our kids, and we're getting there together.' Which statement best evaluates how the language represents values?
options: First-person plural lowers the modality of the claim, so the company avoids committing to any position on air quality
Referring to 'our kids' is an explicit statement of the company's values, so no inference by the reader is required
Inclusive pronouns position the audience as already agreeing with the company, so a shared goal stands in for evidence of action
Inclusive pronouns make the claim measurable, so the audience can check the company's environmental record against it
questions.explanation: 'We' and 'our' fold the audience into the company's position, so agreement is assumed before any argument is made, and the vague 'getting there' offers no verifiable commitment — the values are represented implicitly and the reader is invited to supply the goodwill. The option about explicit statement is the tempting one, but 'our kids' names no value; the reader still has to infer that the company cares about the future. Ask what could actually be checked: a shared feeling is not a testable claim.

questions.stem: A magazine article on youth sport is organised as: a description of rising injury rates, then an explanation of why participation has intensified, then a set of recommended changes to junior competitions. Which organising pattern is this?
options: Claim, rebuttal, restated claim
Problem, cause, solution
Chronological recount
Comparison and contrast
questions.explanation: The article names a difficulty, explains what produces it, then proposes remedies, which is the standard problem-cause-solution pattern used in texts that argue for change. Chronological recount is tempting because the three sections come in order, but a recount would sequence events by time, and rising injury rates are a condition rather than a stage in a timeline. Check whether the sections are ordered by when things happened or by their logical role in an argument.

questions.stem: A feature article is organised as: a problem with local bus services, the causes of that problem, then three proposed solutions. Which organising pattern is this?
options: Compare and contrast
Classification of types
Problem–solution
Chronological recount
questions.explanation: A problem–solution pattern names an issue, explores it, then moves to proposed responses, which suits a purpose of persuading readers that action is needed. 'Chronological recount' is tempting because the article does move forward through stages, but chronology means ordering by time, and this article is ordered by logic rather than by when events happened. Check what governs the order: a clock and calendar means chronological, while an issue followed by remedies means problem–solution.

questions.stem: An essay on social media spends five paragraphs on the benefits and then a single short paragraph on the harms, before concluding that the platforms are largely positive. Which statement best evaluates this organisation?
options: The inclusion of a harms paragraph proves the essay treats both sides of the issue even-handedly
The organisation is faulty because a balanced essay must always give each side an identical number of paragraphs
The structure has no bearing on the argument, since persuasion depends only on the writer's word choices
The unequal proportion of the text given to each side works to make the positive conclusion appear inevitable
questions.explanation: Evaluating structure means judging its effect: giving five paragraphs to one side and one to the other weights the reader's impression before the conclusion arrives, so the verdict feels pre-decided. The option claiming even-handedness is tempting because a counter-view is genuinely present, but mere presence is not balance when the space allocated is so lopsided. Look at proportion and placement, not just whether the other side is mentioned.

questions.stem: In an analytical essay, what is the main job of a topic sentence at the start of a body paragraph?
options: To restate the essay question in different words so the marker can see it was read
To introduce a new subject that the paragraph will contrast with the thesis
To state the idea that the paragraph will develop and link it to the essay's argument
To provide the strongest piece of evidence, usually a quotation, before analysis begins
questions.explanation: A topic sentence signposts the paragraph's controlling idea and shows how it advances the overall argument, which is how writers organise ideas so a reader can follow the line of reasoning. The option about giving the strongest quotation first is tempting because evidence does belong in the paragraph, but evidence supports the idea rather than announcing it, and a paragraph opening with a quotation leaves the reader unsure what it is for. The cue: a topic sentence is a claim in the writer's own voice, not a quotation, restatement or a change of subject.

questions.stem: A writer organises an information report using the pattern: general statement, then classification of types, then description of each type. This pattern is best described as:
options: Problem and solution organisation
General to specific organisation
Chronological organisation
Compare and contrast organisation
questions.explanation: Moving from a broad statement to categories and then to detail within each category is a general-to-specific structure, typical of reports that build a reader's knowledge in layers. Compare and contrast is the tempting choice because listing types looks like setting them side by side, but the text describes each type in turn rather than measuring them against shared criteria. The cue: comparison texts use similarity and difference markers such as 'whereas' or 'both', while general-to-specific texts simply narrow their focus.

questions.stem: A reader is 'monitoring' their comprehension when they:
options: Keep a running list of the unfamiliar vocabulary in the text to look up after reading
Track how the writer's attitude to the subject shifts from the opening to the conclusion
Notice that meaning has broken down and take deliberate action, such as rereading or slowing down
Check the writer's claims against a second source to test whether the argument is accurate
questions.explanation: Monitoring is metacognitive: the reader keeps checking whether they are still understanding and repairs the breakdown when they are not. Checking claims against another source is evaluating the text's reliability, not monitoring your own comprehension — the giveaway is that monitoring is directed at the reader's own understanding, not at the text's accuracy. Ask: who or what is being checked? If it is your own grasp of meaning, it is monitoring.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes an effective summary of a complex argumentative text?
options: A brief account of the central claim and the main supporting reasons, in the reader's own words
An ordered retelling of every point the writer makes, kept in the writer's original wording
A list of the most striking quotations from the text, chosen for their persuasive force
A judgement about whether the writer's argument is convincing and where it is weakest
questions.explanation: Summarising means selecting and condensing: identify the controlling idea and the reasons that carry it, then express them concisely in your own words. Retelling every point in the original wording is the most tempting wrong answer because it feels thorough, but reproducing everything is not condensing and offers no evidence of understanding. Remember that a summary must be shorter than the source and must involve selection.

questions.stem: Which strategy involves using a text's title, headings, opening paragraph and text type to work out what is likely to come next?
options: Predicting
Connecting
Visualising
Questioning
questions.explanation: Predicting uses features already visible — title, headings, structure, genre conventions — to anticipate content, and the reader then confirms or revises the prediction while reading. Connecting is the closest distractor because both draw on prior knowledge, but connecting links the text to other texts, experiences or the wider world rather than forecasting what is ahead. The cue is direction: predicting points forward into the unread text.

questions.stem: While reading an abstract essay about memory, Sofia stops at the end of a paragraph, realises she has read the words without following the reasoning, goes back to the previous paragraph and rereads it more slowly before continuing. Which strategy is she using?
options: Summarising, because she is condensing the paragraph before she moves on
Predicting, because rereading helps her anticipate the essay's next stage
Monitoring, because she detects a breakdown in understanding and repairs it
Inferring, because she is working out a meaning the essay leaves unstated
questions.explanation: The defining move here is Sofia noticing her own loss of meaning and choosing a fix-up action, which is exactly what monitoring means. Inferring is tempting because rereading often leads to an inference, but the described behaviour is the self-check and the repair, not the drawing of an unstated conclusion. Look at what the reader actually does: detect a problem plus act on it equals monitoring.

questions.stem: A speech includes the line: 'We have built a city that runs on light and forgets to sleep.' Which reader response is an inference supported by the text, rather than an unsupported guess?
options: The speaker grew up in a rural town and dislikes living in large Australian cities
The speaker wants street lighting reduced in residential areas to save on council costs
The speaker views constant activity as something the city has created and now cannot switch off
The speaker is arguing that electricity prices in the city have risen faster than wages
questions.explanation: A valid inference stays tethered to the words on the page: 'built', 'runs on light' and 'forgets to sleep' together imply a human-made, unstoppable restlessness. The claim about electricity prices is the most tempting distractor because 'runs on light' sounds like a reference to power use, but nothing in the line mentions cost, wages or pricing at all. Test any inference by asking which specific words force that reading — if you cannot point to them, it is a guess.

questions.stem: While reading a dense essay arguing that privacy is 'a luxury good', Priya writes in the margin: 'Luxury for whom? Who decides what counts as private? What evidence is there that this has changed?' Which comprehension strategy is she mainly using?
options: Visualising, to convert the writer's abstract claim into concrete mental images
Questioning, to interrogate the writer's assumptions and open up the abstract claim
Summarising, to reduce the writer's abstract claim to a manageable set of points
Monitoring, to check whether she has understood the sentences she has just read
questions.explanation: Questioning means generating your own questions about a text — about assumptions, evidence and gaps — in order to probe ideas rather than accept them. Monitoring is the tempting alternative, but monitoring asks 'am I following this?' and leads to rereading or slowing down; Priya's notes are not about her own comprehension breaking down, they are aimed at the writer's argument. The cue is the target of the question: monitoring points at the reader, questioning points at the text.

questions.stem: What does creating a text 'in deliberate consideration of an audience' mainly require?
options: Removing all personal opinion from the text so any reader at all can agree with it
Choosing the most formal register, since formality makes a text suitable
Choosing a topic the audience already agrees with, avoiding disagreement
Shaping vocabulary, tone, examples and structure around what that audience expects
questions.explanation: Considering audience means making specific craft decisions — level of technical vocabulary, degree of formality, choice of examples, how much background to explain — on the basis of who is receiving the text. The most tempting distractor is the one about choosing the most formal register, because formality is often praised in school writing; but a podcast for Year 7 students or a blog for peers is badly served by maximum formality, so the real rule is fit, not formality. Test yourself by asking 'what changes if my reader changes?' — if nothing changes, you have not considered audience.

questions.stem: Which of these is a digital element, available in an online text but not in a printed one?
options: A pull quote that repeats a striking sentence in larger type beside the column
A caption that identifies the people in a photograph and explains what is happening
An embedded hyperlink that takes the reader straight to the source being quoted
A subheading that breaks a long section of the text into shorter labelled parts
questions.explanation: Digital elements depend on the medium's interactivity: hyperlinks, embedded video or audio, comment threads and search functions cannot exist on paper. Subheadings, pull quotes and captions are all print features that have simply been carried across into online layouts, so the pull quote option is tempting if you associate it with news websites. The cue is to ask whether the element requires a reader to click, tap or play something.

questions.stem: A student must create a reflective text about a complex issue — how her thinking about AI writing tools has changed — for the class blog. Which opening sentence best matches a reflective purpose?
options: AI writing tools must be banned from all secondary schools immediately, before more damage is done.
AI writing tools are software programs that generate sentences in response to a user's typed prompt.
This report will outline three findings from a survey of sixty Year 10 students about AI use.
I used to think using an AI tool was simply cheating; a semester of using one has complicated that view.
questions.explanation: A reflective text foregrounds the writer's own thinking over time, so it typically signals a shift, a tension or an unresolved question, which the change from 'used to think' to 'has complicated' does exactly. The banning sentence is the tempting choice because it clearly concerns the same issue, but its high modality and single fixed position make it persuasive writing, not reflection. The cue is whether the sentence shows the writer's thinking moving, or simply asserts a settled conclusion.

questions.stem: Kai has written a print feature article on housing affordability and must now turn the same material into a ten-minute podcast episode for the same audience. Which change best shows him adapting to the new mode?
options: Inserting subheadings and a data graphic before each section so the structure is visible
Lengthening his paragraphs so that each section of the argument is fully developed in one block
Turning his statistic-heavy paragraphs into a short interview and signposting each new section aloud
Adding numbered footnotes so listeners can check the source of every statistic he mentions
questions.explanation: Listeners cannot re-scan a spoken text, so podcast adaptation means replacing visual navigation with audible signposting and breaking up dense data into voices and shorter units. The footnotes option is tempting because citing sources is genuinely good practice, but footnotes are a print apparatus that a listener can never see. Whenever you adapt across modes, ask what the audience can and cannot do in the new mode — here, they can listen but not look.

questions.stem: Mia is writing a letter to her local MP arguing for a bus route to be reinstated. Which of her planning decisions is a consideration of audience rather than of purpose?
options: Choosing to argue a case rather than simply describe what the service used to be
Referring to the MP's recent public statement about transport funding in the electorate
Deciding that the letter's main aim is to have the bus route restored next year
Selecting the strongest three pieces of evidence that support her central claim
questions.explanation: Purpose is what the text is trying to achieve; audience is who receives it and what they already know, believe or have said. Referring to the MP's own statement is a choice made because of who is reading, so it is an audience decision. Deciding the aim is restoration is tempting because it is concrete and specific, but it names the outcome the text pursues, which is purpose by definition. If the decision would change when the reader changes, it is about audience.

questions.stem: For a campaign task, Dev designs an infographic on food waste that contains twelve statistics, three charts, and a paragraph beside each chart restating the same figures in words. Which feedback best improves its multimodal design?
options: Convert the whole infographic into slides so the paragraphs can be read aloud to the audience
Expand the introduction so that every chart is fully explained in words before the reader sees it
Cut the repeated wording so the charts carry the data and the text adds what images cannot show
Add several more statistics beside each chart, since a greater volume of data increases credibility
questions.explanation: Effective multimodal design gives each mode distinct work: visuals handle comparison and proportion, while written text supplies context, interpretation or a call to action that images cannot convey. Duplicating the figures in prose wastes space and slows the reader without adding meaning. The suggestion to expand the introduction is tempting because explanation sounds helpful, but it multiplies exactly the redundancy that is the problem. The test is whether removing one element would lose meaning — if not, it is repetition.

questions.stem: A Year 10 task asks for a text that 'reflects on a challenging and complex issue'. Which feature most clearly shows genuine engagement with complexity?
options: Restating the writer's existing position more forcefully, using stronger emotive vocabulary throughout
Summarising the views of three published sources in turn without adding the writer's own reasoning
Naming a real tension between two defensible positions and explaining how the writer weighs them
Setting out arguments for and against at equal length and leaving the two lists side by side
questions.explanation: Complexity is shown by grappling — identifying why reasonable people disagree and then reasoning towards a considered position, including what the writer concedes. The balanced-lists option is the most tempting, because balance looks fair and thorough, but merely placing two sets of points beside each other leaves the intellectual work undone; nothing is weighed. Look for connectives of concession and evaluation, such as 'although' or 'this matters more because', as evidence that thinking is actually happening.

questions.stem: Which task is proofreading rather than revising?
options: Adding statistical evidence to an unsupported claim
Correcting subject–verb agreement errors in three sentences
Moving the final paragraph so it appears second
Deleting an argument that repeats an earlier point
questions.explanation: Proofreading deals with surface accuracy — grammar, spelling, punctuation — without changing what the text says or how it is built. Moving the final paragraph is a revision of organisation, and deleting a repeated argument or adding evidence changes content. The cue: if the meaning or the structure changes, it is revision; if only correctness changes, it is proofreading.

questions.stem: In editing, what does it mean to check a text for coherence?
options: Checking that sentence lengths vary enough to keep the reader's attention
Checking that formal vocabulary is used consistently from the opening to the close
Checking that ideas connect and the whole text holds together logically for a reader
Checking that spelling, punctuation and apostrophes are accurate throughout the text
questions.explanation: Coherence is about the sense a reader makes of the text as a whole: ideas ordered so each one follows from the last, with links that show how parts relate. The option about spelling and punctuation describes proofreading for accuracy, which can be perfect in a text whose argument still jumps around incoherently. The cue is that coherence is measured at the level of the whole text and the reader's understanding, not at the level of individual errors or word choices.

questions.stem: Which group of connectives all signal a contrast between ideas in an argument?
options: therefore, consequently, as a result
furthermore, moreover, in addition
for example, for instance, such as
however, nevertheless, on the other hand
questions.explanation: Contrastive connectives tell the reader that what follows qualifies or opposes what came before, which is how a writer signals a counter-argument or a shift in position. The set beginning with 'therefore' is tempting because those words also join paragraphs, but they signal cause and effect: the second idea results from the first. Ask what relationship the word claims — opposition, result, addition or illustration — before using it to link paragraphs.

questions.stem: A paragraph reads: 'The river was dredged in 2019. The fish numbers fell. Locals complained to council. The council ordered a report.' Which revision best improves control of sentence structure here?
options: Rewrite each sentence in the passive voice so that the paragraph sounds more formal and objective
Add two or three descriptive adjectives to every noun so the writing becomes more vivid
Turn the first and third sentences into rhetorical questions so the reader is drawn into the events
Combine some sentences using subordinate clauses so the causal links between the events are made explicit
questions.explanation: The run of short simple sentences states four events but leaves the reader to guess how they relate; subordination ('After the river was dredged in 2019, fish numbers fell...') encodes cause, time and consequence inside the sentence. Shifting everything to passive voice is tempting because passive constructions are common in formal reports, but it hides who acted without solving the real problem, which is missing connection between ideas. Ask first whether the relationships between ideas are visible, then worry about tone.

questions.stem: A submission to council contains the sentence: 'The council totally dropped the ball on the drainage upgrade.' Which edit best refines the vocabulary for this purpose and audience?
options: The council did not meet the completion dates it published for the drainage upgrade.
The council really messed up the drainage upgrade in a pretty big way.
The council, sadly, did not do a great job with the drainage upgrade at all.
The council dropped the ball, so to speak, on the drainage upgrade project.
questions.explanation: A formal submission needs a claim that is precise enough to be checked, so replacing the idiom with a specific, verifiable statement about missed published dates suits both the purpose and the official readership. The version keeping 'dropped the ball, so to speak' is the trap: adding a hedge does not remove the informal idiom, it draws attention to it. Test an edit by asking whether the new wording is both formal and more specific, not merely softer.

questions.stem: During a class discussion of a persuasive article, what is the main purpose of asking a clarifying question?
options: To show the group that the speaker's interpretation of the article is mistaken
To move the discussion on to a point you had prepared before the discussion began
To correct a speaker's expression so their contribution sounds more formal
To check that you have understood a speaker's meaning accurately before you respond to it
questions.explanation: A clarifying question ('Do you mean the writer's tone, or the writer's evidence?') exists to secure shared understanding so that agreement or disagreement is based on what was actually said. Signalling that a speaker is wrong is the tempting choice, but that is a challenge or rebuttal, not clarification — clarifying is neutral about who is right. The cue is direction: clarifying asks for information back from the speaker, rather than delivering a judgement to them.

questions.stem: A memoir chapter opens and closes with the narrator standing at the same kitchen window. What is the most likely effect of this structural choice?
options: It tells the reader that the narrator's account of events cannot be trusted
It shows that the chapter is factual writing rather than a personal reflection
It invites the reader to measure what has changed in the narrator between the two moments
It signals to the reader that the events of the chapter are told out of chronological order
questions.explanation: A cyclic or framing structure repeats an image so the reader compares the two versions of the same scene, which foregrounds change (or its absence) in the narrator. The suggestion that events are told out of order is tempting because repetition can accompany flashback, but repeating a setting at the start and end says nothing in itself about the sequence of events. The cue is that structure creates comparison; disordered time would need actual shifts in the timeline.

questions.stem: A student says 'I'd argue the ending is more hopeful than it appears'. What does that framing do?
options: It makes the claim stronger than a statement of fact, so listeners must accept it
It removes the speaker's viewpoint so the group can stay neutral
It signals the speaker has not read the text closely enough
It presents the claim as open to challenge, inviting others to test it
questions.explanation: Tentative or hedged phrasing such as 'I'd argue' marks the statement as an interpretation being offered for discussion, which invites other students to respond, extend or disagree productively. The idea that it makes the claim stronger than fact reverses how modality works — hedging lowers the force of a claim rather than raising it. Watch for the wording: 'I'd argue' and 'it seems' soften, while 'clearly' and 'must' harden.

questions.stem: A documentary about gambling advertising presents five personal stories of loss, and only in the final minute reveals the total amount spent on such advertising in Australia each year. Which analysis of this structural choice is best supported?
options: Opening with personal stories keeps the documentary neutral, because no argument is being made until the statistic appears
The structure is chronological, since it traces the growth of gambling advertising from its beginnings to the present day
Withholding the figure means viewers meet the human cost first, so the statistic arrives as confirmation of a response already built
Placing the figure last shows the filmmakers judged it their weakest evidence and hoped most viewers would overlook it
questions.explanation: Sequencing is a persuasive choice: emotional material placed first shapes how later evidence is received, so the final statistic reads as proof of a feeling the viewer already holds. The 'keeps the documentary neutral' option is tempting because personal stories can seem like plain reporting, but selecting and ordering five stories of loss is itself an argument. Ask what each stage prepares the audience to feel or accept, not just what information it contains.

questions.stem: During a class discussion of a novel, Amara says: "Building on what Tom said about the ending, I think the last image of the empty boat also picks up the flood scene in chapter two." Which interaction skill is she mainly using?
options: Restating a peer's point in different words to show she was listening
Redirecting the discussion to a new topic she has prepared in advance
Withdrawing her own reading of the text in favour of Tom's reading
Extending a peer's point by adding further textual evidence to it
questions.explanation: Amara names Tom's contribution and then adds new evidence (the boat image and the flood scene) that develops his idea further, which is what extending or building on a contribution means. Restating a peer's point in different words is only paraphrasing — it adds no new evidence or reasoning, and Amara clearly adds both. The cue is the word 'also' followed by fresh detail from the text: paraphrase repeats, extension adds.

questions.stem: Which of these choices in a persuasive article is a text structure choice rather than a language feature?
options: Ordering the argument so the strongest point is saved for the final section
Choosing emotive adjectives such as 'devastating' to describe the flood damage
Using the inclusive pronoun 'we' to position readers as part of the solution
Describing the council's plan with the metaphor of a house built on sand
questions.explanation: Text structure refers to how a whole text is organised and sequenced — including the order of sections and where the strongest material is placed. Emotive adjectives, inclusive pronouns and metaphors are all choices made at the level of words and sentences, so they are language features, even though they help build the argument. The cue is scope: if you could only see the choice by looking at the shape of the whole text, it is structure.

questions.stem: A feature article about a factory closure opens on the workers' final shift, then moves backwards through the plant's forty-year history, ending with its opening day in 1984. Which analysis of this structural choice is best supported?
options: Reversing the chronology signals to readers that the account is imagined rather than based on real events and people
Beginning with the closure frames the whole history as loss, so readers interpret each earlier event as leading towards that ending
Reversing the chronology removes the writer's viewpoint, leaving readers with a neutral record of the factory's history
Reversing the chronology confuses the sequence of events, so the article cannot achieve a persuasive or reflective purpose
questions.explanation: Placing the outcome first gives readers a frame: everything that follows is read in the light of the closure, so ordinary past events take on the weight of loss and inevitability. The claim that reverse order makes the text neutral is the most tempting error, but sequencing is itself an authorial choice — deciding what readers know first is a way of shaping attitude, not removing it. Ask what readers know at each stage and how that knowledge colours what comes next.

questions.stem: Which list contains only features of voice that a speaker can control during delivery?
options: Pace, pitch, volume and pausing
Gesture, posture, eye contact and facial expression
Font size, slide colour, layout and animation
Topic sentences, connectives, paragraphing and headings
questions.explanation: Features of voice are the vocal choices a speaker makes as they speak — how fast (pace), how high or low (pitch), how loud (volume) and where silence is placed (pausing) — plus tone and stress. The list of gesture, posture, eye contact and facial expression is tempting because these are also delivery skills, but they are non-verbal body language, not voice. The cue: if it can still be heard on an audio recording with no picture, it is a feature of voice.

questions.stem: Which of these is a multimodal element added to a spoken presentation?
options: A rhetorical question asked twice for emphasis
A three-second pause before the final sentence
An anecdote about the speaker's own experience
A short projected video clip that plays behind the speaker
questions.explanation: Multimodal means combining modes — here the spoken mode plus moving image and sound, which the projected clip provides. A three-second pause is tempting because it is a deliberate crafted effect, but it operates entirely within the spoken mode, so it is a feature of voice rather than a second mode. Check whether an extra mode (visual, audio, digital) has actually been introduced.

questions.stem: Nina is delivering a three-minute persuasive speech to her class. She wants listeners to be able to follow her argument without a written copy in front of them. Which structural choice best supports this?
options: Placing all of her statistics together in one dense central section
Using longer, more complex sentences so the argument sounds thoroughly developed
Signposting the number of points at the start and naming each one as she reaches it
Reading from a full script so that no sentence is accidentally left out
questions.explanation: Listeners cannot re-read, so spoken texts need audible signposts — previewing how many points are coming and naming each transition — to hold the structure in memory. Reading from a full script is tempting because it guarantees complete content, but it does not make the structure audible and usually flattens delivery. The test for spoken structure: could a listener say afterwards how many points there were and what they were?

questions.stem: Riya's speech to a local business breakfast about youth employment is entirely formal, but at one point she says: 'And then — nothing. No callback, no email, nothing.' Which statement best evaluates this shift?
options: The brief informal shift is effective because it uses the contrast with the formal register to make one moment feel personal
The shift is a lapse, because a spoken text must maintain a single consistent register throughout to remain credible
The shift is effective because informal language is always more persuasive than formal language for adult audiences
The shift is a lapse, because fragments are grammatical errors that cannot be used deliberately in a speech
questions.explanation: Experimenting with formality includes controlled shifts: a short informal, fragmented moment inside a formal speech stands out precisely because it breaks the established register, creating emphasis and immediacy. The claim that a spoken text must keep one register throughout is tempting because consistency is often praised, but deliberate variation is a recognised craft choice when it is purposeful and brief. Ask whether the shift is controlled and motivated, or accidental and sustained.

questions.stem: Mid-speech, Jordan states a statistic then pauses for two seconds. Why?
options: It signals to the audience that Jordan has lost their place in the speech
It lowers the formality of the speech by breaking the flow of the argument
It replaces emphasis, since a pause carries no meaning itself
It gives the audience a moment to absorb the statistic
questions.explanation: Pausing is a feature of voice used for emphasis: silence after a key point isolates it from the surrounding words and gives listeners processing time, which is why practised speakers pause deliberately after statistics or claims. The idea that it signals losing his place confuses a controlled, planned pause with an unplanned hesitation — the cue is that a deliberate pause comes immediately after important content, not mid-sentence. Formality is set by word choice and grammar, not by pausing, and pausing is itself a form of emphasis rather than a substitute for it.

questions.stem: In a Year 10 speaking task, what does 'experimenting with formality' in a spoken text mainly involve?
options: Removing every contraction and personal pronoun from the whole speech
Speaking more slowly and loudly than you would in ordinary conversation
Adjusting vocabulary, sentence style and tone to suit the audience and situation
Using the longest and most technical words available throughout the speech
questions.explanation: Formality (register) is a matter of language choice — how technical or everyday the vocabulary is, how tightly structured the sentences are, and how distant or personal the tone is — and it is adjusted according to who is listening and why. Choosing the longest words available is the most tempting distractor, but formality is about appropriateness to context, and unnecessarily technical wording often fails a general audience. Volume and pace are features of voice, which are separate from register; the cue is that formality lives in the words on the page, delivery features in how they are spoken.

questions.stem: Amira is presenting a five-minute proposal to the school council and will use slides. Which slide design best supports her spoken delivery?
options: A short heading, one image or graph, and three key phrases she then expands on aloud
Her full script in paragraphs, so she can read it accurately to the council
A single decorative photograph on every slide with no text or data at all
Every statistic she mentions, listed on one slide so nothing is left out
questions.explanation: In a multimodal presentation the slides support the spoken text rather than duplicate it, so brief cues plus one visual let the audience listen while the speaker does the explaining. Putting the full script on the slides is the most tempting option because it feels safe, but the audience will read ahead instead of listening and the delivery becomes a reading rather than a presentation. Purely decorative slides give the audience nothing to follow, and a dense wall of statistics competes with the speaker's voice for attention.

questions.stem: Speaking to a public forum about local flood planning, Tessa plays a 30-second recorded interview with a resident, then explains how it supports her second argument. Which evaluation of this choice is best supported?
options: The recording counts as a feature of voice rather than a multimodal element in her presentation
Including a digital element makes the presentation informal, so it no longer suits a public forum
It adds an authentic supporting voice and varies the delivery, and her framing keeps it tied to her argument
The clip removes any need for Tessa to state a claim, because the evidence speaks for itself to the forum
questions.explanation: A well-integrated digital element works as evidence and as a change of texture in the delivery, but only when the speaker explicitly links it back to the claim it supports — which is exactly what Tessa's follow-up explanation does. The idea that evidence speaks for itself is tempting, but an unframed clip leaves the audience to guess its relevance; in argument, the speaker must interpret evidence. A recording is a multimodal element, since features of voice are aspects of the speaker's own delivery, and digital elements can be used in highly formal contexts without lowering register.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say a text's representation of people and events 'reflects context'?
options: The text must supply factual background about its setting so readers can follow it
The meaning depends on the reader's mood, so no two readers analyse it alike
It only reflects context when the writer states their own beliefs openly
How people and events are portrayed carries traces of the time, place and values
questions.explanation: A representation is a set of choices — what to include, what to leave out, which words to use — and those choices are shaped by the attitudes, assumptions and circumstances of the time and place of writing, so analysing them tells us about context. The option about supplying factual background confuses 'context' with 'background information given to the reader'; context is the surrounding social, cultural and historical situation of the text, not a section inside it. The cue: context is about the conditions that produced the choices, not the detail printed on the page.

questions.stem: A news report describes a demonstration as 'a mob of activists swarming the steps of parliament'. A second report on the same event describes 'residents gathering outside parliament'. Which statement best analyses how these language choices represent attitudes?
options: Both reports simply name who was present and what they did, so neither set of choices represents an attitude towards the protesters at all.
The second report is the more emotive of the two, because 'residents' and 'gathering' are technical terms that exaggerate the size of the crowd.
The first report represents its attitude explicitly, because labelling a group as a 'mob' is a factual claim about numbers rather than a connotation.
The noun 'mob' and the verb 'swarming' carry negative connotations, implicitly representing the protesters as an irrational threat rather than as citizens.
questions.explanation: Values and attitudes are often carried implicitly through connotation: 'mob' and 'swarming' (an insect-like verb) position the group as disorderly and menacing, while 'residents gathering' positions the same people as ordinary locals exercising a right. The option claiming the first report is 'explicit' is the most tempting, because the words are certainly loaded — but explicit representation means the attitude is stated outright, such as 'this protest was reckless'; here the judgement is smuggled in through word choice. The cue: if you have to unpack connotations to reach the attitude, the representation is implicit.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a persuasive text?
options: To tell an entertaining story
To record events in the order they happened
To convince the reader of a position
To explain how something works
questions.explanation: A persuasive text sets out to move the reader towards a view. Explaining how something works is an expository purpose, and a text can inform without trying to persuade at all.
questions.teaching:
Texts are usually sorted by what they are trying to do, and the main purposes are worth having in mind as a set.

Some inform or explain, setting out how something works without asking you to agree. Some narrate, telling a story to entertain. Some recount, laying out events in the order they happened. And some set out to move the reader towards a position — an editorial, an advertisement, a speech at an assembly. That last purpose is the one being asked about, and it is what makes techniques like rhetorical questions, emotive language and repetition worth looking for.

questions.stem: What is a text's audience?
options: The subject it is about
The readers it is written for
The person who actually wrote it
The place it was published
questions.explanation: The audience is who the text is aimed at, and it shapes vocabulary, tone and how much background gets explained. Confusing audience with author is the usual slip.
questions.teaching:
Three things are always worth establishing about a text, and it is easy to answer the wrong one under time pressure.

Who made it is the author or composer. What it is about is the subject. And who it was made for is the audience — the readers or viewers the writer had in mind, which shapes vocabulary, tone, how much background gets explained and which examples get chosen. A science article for specialists and one for a newspaper can cover the same subject and look nothing alike, and the difference is almost entirely this. It is the question that explains most of a text's choices.

questions.stem: What does 'skimming' a text mean?
options: Reading aloud to an audience
Reading only the final paragraph
Reading quickly for the general idea
Reading closely for exact detail
questions.explanation: Skimming moves fast to get the gist. Scanning is the related skill, hunting for one specific piece of information, and the two are easily swapped.
questions.teaching:
Two fast reading techniques get taught together and are easy to swap, so it helps to pin down what each is looking for.

One moves quickly over the whole text — headings, opening sentences, the shape of it — to get a general sense of what it is about and whether it is worth reading properly. The other hunts for one specific thing, like running your eye down a page for a date or a name, ignoring everything else. The first is about the whole at low detail; the second is about one detail while ignoring the whole. Neither is careful reading, which is a third thing again.

questions.stem: What is an inference?
options: A fact the text states directly and openly
A summary of the whole text
A question asked about the text
A conclusion drawn from clues in the text
questions.explanation: An inference is a reasoned conclusion the text implies without stating. If you can point at a sentence that says it outright, that is a stated fact rather than an inference.
questions.teaching:
Comprehension questions usually work at two levels, and knowing which level is being asked for saves a lot of trouble.

Some answers are stated outright, and you can point at the sentence containing them. Others are not stated anywhere, but the text gives you enough to work them out — a character's slammed door and short replies tell you they are angry without the word appearing. Drawing that conclusion from evidence is what this question is about. The test is simple: if you can quote a line that says it, it was stated; if you had to put clues together, it was not.

questions.stem: What is the tone of a text?
options: The feeling created in the reader
The order the ideas are arranged in
The number of paragraphs it uses
The writer's attitude to the subject
questions.explanation: Tone is the writer's stance — angry, admiring, sceptical. Mood is the tempting near-miss: that is what the reader feels. Ask whose feeling is being described.
questions.teaching:
This pairs with mood, and separating them comes down to one question: whose feeling is being described?

One of the two is the writer's attitude towards their subject — you might describe it as bitter, admiring, wry, or coolly neutral. It comes through in word choice, sentence length and what gets emphasised or left out. The other is what the reader ends up feeling, the atmosphere created. So a writer can adopt a detached, flat tone precisely in order to produce a mood of dread. Deciding which the question wants tells you where to look: at the writer's choices, or at your own response.

questions.stem: What is a topic sentence?
options: The sentence that contains a direct quotation
The sentence stating a paragraph's main idea
The first sentence of the whole text
The longest sentence in a paragraph
questions.explanation: A topic sentence announces what its paragraph is about, usually at the start. Every paragraph can have one, so it is not the opening line of the text as a whole.
questions.teaching:
Paragraphs in non-fiction usually have a structure, and there is a standard name for the sentence that announces what the paragraph is about.

It normally sits at the start, states the main idea in general terms, and the rest of the paragraph then supports it with evidence, examples and explanation. Every paragraph can have one, which is why it is not the same as the opening line of the whole text. The practical use is in skimming: read only these across a long article and you get its argument. Writing them well is also the fastest way to make an essay easier to follow.

questions.stem: What is a secondary source?
options: An interview with a witness
An account written after the events
A record made at the time by a witness
A photograph taken on the day
questions.explanation: A secondary source interprets events after they happened. Anything created at the time — a photograph, a diary, a witness interview — is primary, which is why three of these options belong together.
questions.teaching:
Sources are classified by their relationship in time to the events they describe, and that is the only test.

Anything created at the time by someone involved or present is primary — letters, diaries, photographs, film footage, objects, official records made on the day. Anything produced afterwards, interpreting and drawing on those, is the other category: a textbook, a documentary, a historian's article. This question has one option standing apart from three that group together, which is worth noticing. Neither type is more reliable in general; each has to be judged on who made it and why.

questions.stem: What does 'bias' in a text mean?
options: A slant favouring one side of an issue
A factual mistake in the information presented
A complex sentence structure
A formal choice of vocabulary
questions.explanation: Bias is a leaning towards one position, shown through selection and wording rather than through errors. A biased text can be entirely accurate, which is why the factual-mistake option is wrong.
questions.teaching:
Bias is not the same as error, and the difference matters when analysing a text.

A biased text leans towards one side of an issue. It shows in what gets included and left out, which words are chosen — "protesters" or "mob", "reduction" or "cut" — whose voices are quoted, and what gets treated as obvious. Crucially, every individual fact in it can be entirely accurate, which is exactly why it is worth spotting: you cannot detect it by fact-checking alone. All texts have a perspective, so the useful question is not whether it is present but what it is and what it does to the reader.
